title: How I structure React components for long-lived UI
description: A practical breakdown of containers, presentational components, data boundaries, and design token usage.
hero: Component architecture is less about folders and more about controlling change. The goal is to make product behavior easy to extend without making the interface fragile.

sections.heading: Start with ownership boundaries
body: I separate components by responsibility before I separate them by visual size. A component that fetches, filters, formats, and renders data is doing too much even if the file is short.
For long-lived UI, I prefer route-level screens, feature containers, reusable view components, and small primitives. This gives each layer a reason to exist.

sections.heading: Keep data transformation close to the feature
body: Generic utilities are useful, but moving every transformation into a shared helper too early makes the codebase harder to follow. I keep feature-specific shaping close to the feature until there is real reuse.
The test is simple: if another feature can use the same function without understanding the original screen, it may deserve to be shared.

sections.heading: Design tokens reduce negotiation
body: A tokenized UI removes repeated decisions from daily implementation. Instead of choosing a border color, shadow, radius, and text color each time, the component chooses from a known visual language.
This is why the portfolio uses semantic classes like glass-panel, section-title, control-button, and technical-label.

takeaways: Name components by responsibility, not only by appearance.
Keep feature logic close until reuse is obvious.
Use semantic styling primitives to keep the UI consistent.
